blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: How an agricultural system works - its inputs, processes and outputs - and the farming types that describe it; then the causes and effects of food shortages and the solutions tried.

blocks.heading: An agricultural system has three parts
blocks.text: Every farm is a system with three parts. Inputs are what goes into the farm: physical inputs such as sunshine, rain and soil; human inputs of labour, skill and money; and bought inputs such as seed, fertiliser, tools and fuel. Processes are what the farmer does on the farm: clearing, ploughing, sowing, weeding, irrigating, harvesting, feeding, milking. Outputs are what comes out: products for the family or the market, and waste such as straw, dung and run-off. The test for any item is whether it goes in or comes out: a bag of fertiliser is an input, and the maize it helps grow is an output.

blocks.heading: Four pairs of farming terms
blocks.text: Farms are described with four independent pairs of terms. Subsistence farming feeds the farmer's family, with little or nothing sold; commercial farming sells its produce for profit. Arable farming grows crops; pastoral farming keeps animals. Intensive farming uses high inputs of labour or capital per hectare, giving high yields from a small area; extensive farming uses low inputs per hectare over a large area. Because the pairs are independent, a farm can be any combination at once: a family's maize garden is subsistence, arable and intensive; a Karakul sheep run in the Namib is commercial, pastoral and extensive.

blocks.heading: A worked system: a northern maize garden
blocks.text: A maize garden beside a homestead in the north of Namibia shows the system in the round. Inputs: rain in the wet months, household labour, seed kept from last year's harvest, a hand hoe, and cattle manure. Processes: the ground is cleared and hoed, seed is sown at the first rains, the plot is weeded, and birds are scared from the ripening cobs. Outputs: cobs eaten fresh, meal ground for the family, stovers fed to cattle, and waste to the compost. The classification follows by itself: subsistence (food for the family), arable (a crop is grown), intensive (much labour on a small plot).

blocks.heading: The causes of food shortages
blocks.text: Food shortages have natural causes and human causes, and a full answer names both kinds. Natural: drought that withers crops and pasture; floods that drown fields and wash away soil; tropical storms that flatten a season's work; and pests and diseases - locust swarms and army worm can strip a district's standing crops in days. Human: war and displacement, which keep fields un-planted; poor transport, which strands food in surplus regions while deficit regions go hungry; and low investment in irrigation, storage and farming skills, which keeps yields small. The two kinds also feed one another: land degraded by overuse fails faster when the rains fail.

blocks.heading: From shortage to suffering: the chain of effects
blocks.text: The effects of a shortage follow a chain. A harvest fails or food cannot reach people, so the food available becomes scarcer and prices rise. Families can afford less, so they eat less; undernutrition rises, and children suffer first - growth falters and resistance to disease drops, so illness and death rates rise. Families then sell assets or leave their land to find work or food, and the loss of assets deepens poverty after the crisis ends. Each link is a consequence of the one before it, which is why effects are named after the shortage and are not causes of it.

blocks.heading: Solutions: supply and access together
blocks.text: Solutions work on both sides of the balance. On the supply side: irrigation cuts dependence on rain; better seed and fertiliser raise yields per hectare; pest control protects the standing crop; and roads and storage cut post-harvest losses. On the access side: grain reserves and food aid bridge a bad season; family planning slows population growth where it outstrips the land; and new trades give families money to buy food grown elsewhere. Judging a solution means asking how well it fits the place: irrigation raises yields, but it costs money that small farmers may not have; food aid saves lives, but as cheap grain it can undercut the local growers the region needs next season.

blocks.heading: Natural or human; cause or effect
blocks.text: Two sorting errors appear again and again. The first is giving human causes when natural causes are asked for - answering "war" to a question about drought - or the reverse. The second is giving causes when effects are asked: rising prices and undernutrition are what the shortage causes, not what causes it. The fix is to ask of every point: natural or human, and cause or effect? Drought is a natural cause; war is a human cause; hungry families are an effect.

blocks.heading: Where this connects
blocks.text: Food production carries the development ideas of topic 3.1 - subsistence farming belongs to the low-income, primary-heavy employment structure described there - and it links forward to industry (3.3), which processes farm outputs, to tourism (3.4) on Namibia's farms and lodges, to water (3.6) for irrigation, and to the environmental risks of economic development (3.7). The population topics supply the demand side of the food balance.
